opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to look at it in roughly three stages.

The first is the symbolic AI era. The original dream of AI, going back to the 1950s and 60s, was basically an agent: a system that perceives an environment, reasons, and acts to achieve goals. But the way people built them was by hand-writing rules and logic. You had expert systems, planning systems like STRIPS, and so on. The problem was that the world is too messy. You can't write rules for everything, so these systems were very brittle. They worked in narrow, well-defined domains and broke the moment you stepped outside.

The second stage is reinforcement learning, especially deep RL. Around 2015 to 2020, things like Atari, AlphaGo, and robotics showed that you could learn behavior from reward instead of writing rules. That was a big step. But those agents were very specialized. An agent trained on Go can't play Atari, let alone browse the web or write code. And they needed huge amounts of interaction in a simulator. So you got superhuman performance in closed environments but very little generalization.

What changed with large language models is that we finally got something like priors: a broad, general understanding of the world, learned from human text. And more importantly, language gives the agent a way to reason. When I worked on ReAct, the core observation was simple: if you let the model think in language before it acts, interleaving reasoning with actions, it can handle new tasks it was never trained on. Reasoning becomes a kind of action. It doesn't change the external world, but it changes the agent's internal state, and that turns out to be incredibly powerful for generalization.

So in a sense we came full circle. Symbolic AI wanted reasoning but didn't have learning. RL had learning but lacked general priors and reasoning. LLM-based agents combine the two: pretrained knowledge, reasoning in language, and now increasingly RL on top.

I think this also changes what the important questions are. For a long time the bottleneck was methods. Can we build a model that's smart enough? Now the methods are, to a surprising degree, general. The harder questions are what tasks and environments we should put agents in, how we evaluate whether they're actually useful, and how they interact with real people and the real world. That's why I've said we may be entering the "second half" of AI. The first half was about building better models and climbing benchmarks. The second half is more about defining the right problems and making these agents create real value.

r001.rationale: It says the world is too messy to write rules for everything, making symbolic systems brittle and narrow.

r002.rationale: It says an agent trained on Go cannot play Atari or generalize to browsing the web or writing code.

r003.rationale: It mentions heavy simulator interaction and limited generalization, but does not connect replayable environments to difficulty finding real-world applications.

r004.rationale: It links reasoning in language before acting to handling new tasks the agent was never trained on.

r005.rationale: It discusses methods changing over time and separately raises task and environment choice as a newer question, but does not present both as complementary dimensions of agent evolution.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the word "agent" has been around much longer than people realize, and the meaning has shifted a lot. If you open the classic AI textbook, Russell and Norvig, the whole book is framed around agents: something that perceives an environment and takes actions in it. So from the very beginning, "agent" wasn't a new concept, it was almost the definition of AI itself.

In the symbolic era, an agent was basically a rule system. You had explicit representations of the world, logic, planning, search. Things like expert systems, or early planners like STRIPS. The strength was that the behavior was interpretable and you could reason about it formally. The weakness was that it couldn't handle the messiness of the real world. The moment the environment didn't match your hand-written symbols, the whole thing broke. There was no way to generalize.

Then the second wave, which is where I spent part of my PhD, was deep reinforcement learning. Atari, AlphaGo, that whole period. The agent became a neural network trained from scratch on reward. That solved the brittleness problem in a narrow sense, because you learn from interaction rather than hand-coding. But it created a different problem: every environment needed its own agent, trained from zero, with millions or billions of samples. There was no prior knowledge. If you trained an agent to play one game, it knew nothing about any other game, and certainly nothing about language or the human world.

What changed with large language models is that for the first time you have a prior. The model already knows an enormous amount about how the world works, how people communicate, how tools and code behave. So the question flipped. Instead of "how do we learn everything from scratch in this environment," it became "how do we take this huge amount of knowledge and connect it to actions."

That was really the motivation behind ReAct. The observation was simple: reasoning and acting had been studied separately. Chain-of-thought was reasoning without touching the world, and traditional agents were acting without any explicit reasoning. But if you look at how a person solves a task, they interleave the two. You think a bit, you check something, you update your plan. Language models made that natural because the "thought" and the "action" can both just be text.

So I'd summarize the evolution as three shifts. First, from hand-written rules to learned behavior. Second, from learning narrowly per environment to having a general prior. And third, and this is the part I find most interesting, language became the action space itself. In the symbolic era, language was a thing you parsed. In the RL era, it mostly didn't exist. Now the agent thinks in language, acts in language, and even its memory and tools are expressed in language. That's a very different kind of agent, and I think we're still early in figuring out what that actually implies.

r001.rationale: It says symbolic agents were brittle when real-world conditions differed from their hand-written symbols, but does not identify exhaustive rule enumeration as impossible or as the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says an agent trained on one game knew nothing about other games, clearly communicating lack of transfer between environments.

r003.rationale: It mentions high sample requirements for deep RL but does not link dependence on replayable environments to difficulty finding real-world applications.

r004.rationale: It describes reasoning interleaved with actions, but does not attribute operation in new digital environments to agents’ reasoning capabilities.

r005.rationale: It describes changes in learning methods and generality across environments, but does not present changes in methods and task environments as complementary dimensions of agent evolution.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a continuity in the goal, but a big change in how we get there. An agent is a system that perceives an environment, makes decisions, and takes actions to achieve some objective. That idea is much older than large language models.

In symbolic AI, we tried to make those capabilities explicit. We would define the states, the actions, the rules, and then use search or planning to find a solution. That works very well when the world can be described precisely. The difficulty is that the real world doesn’t come with a clean symbolic description. Someone has to decide what matters and encode it, and that becomes a bottleneck.

Learning-based approaches shifted more of that burden from human-written rules to experience. With reinforcement learning, for example, an agent can learn a policy through interaction. But building an agent that transfers across many different tasks and environments has remained difficult.

Large language models give us a different starting point. They learn from language that already contains a huge amount of knowledge about the world, including descriptions of goals, actions, and consequences. So instead of building a separate representation for every task, we can often describe the task in language. The model can then use language to reason about what to do and interact through tools.

The key step, though, is closing the loop. A model producing a plan is not the same as an agent successfully carrying it out. It needs to take an action, observe what actually happened, and revise its next step. Reasoning helps guide action, and action brings back information that can improve the reasoning.

So I wouldn’t say symbolic AI has simply been replaced. Search, planning, and structured representations are still useful. What’s changed is that language models provide a much more flexible interface between those methods and the messy real world. The challenge is turning that flexibility into reliable behavior over many steps.

r001.rationale: It calls manual encoding a bottleneck, but does not clearly state that explicit rules cannot cover every real-world situation.

r002.rationale: It says transfer across many tasks and environments is difficult, but does not state that deep reinforcement-learning agents generally fail to transfer learning from one environment to another.

r003.rationale: It does not mention dependence on endlessly replayable environments or the resulting difficulty finding real-world applications.

r004.rationale: It says language models can reason about actions and use tools, but does not link that reasoning to operating in new digital environments.

r005.rationale: It discusses changes in agent-building methods and the messy real world, but does not present changes in methods and in the tasks or environments agents tackle as complementary dimensions of evolution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the continuity is that AI has always been about building agents: systems that perceive an environment, make decisions, and take actions toward a goal. What has changed is how we represent knowledge and how we produce those decisions.

In symbolic AI, we explicitly represented the world with symbols and rules, and used search or planning to decide what to do. That can work very well when the environment is clearly defined. The difficulty is that the real world is hard to encode. Even a seemingly simple task can require a huge amount of background knowledge, and writing all of that down becomes a bottleneck.

Large language models change this because they learn a lot of knowledge and patterns of reasoning from data. Language also becomes a flexible interface: you can describe a goal, provide observations, and let the model generate a plan or a tool call without designing a separate symbolic representation for every task. That makes it much easier to build agents that operate across different environments.

But a language model by itself is not necessarily an agent. The important step is putting it into a loop: observe, decide, act, and use feedback to decide again. And the old problems are still there—planning, memory, uncertainty, learning from mistakes. So I see LLM agents less as a complete break with symbolic AI and more as a new foundation that lets us revisit those problems with much broader capabilities. We still need structure and verification; we just don’t have to handcraft all the knowledge.

r001.rationale: It says the real world is hard to encode, that simple tasks can require huge amounts of background knowledge, and that writing it all down becomes a bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss deep reinforcement learning agents or their ability to transfer learning between environments.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention replayable environments or difficulty applying deep reinforcement learning to real-world settings.

r004.rationale: It says LLM agents can operate across different environments, but does not clearly attribute that ability specifically to their reasoning capabilities in new digital environments.

r005.rationale: The response discusses changes in knowledge representation and broader environments, but does not present these as complementary dimensions of agent evolution.
